title: Relay chariots
hookLine: seven chariots in relay, each for one stage of the road

lines: A GROVE, A TREE, AN AFTERNOON.
cards: Two monks have heard of each other and never met. One is Sariputta, the Buddha's chief disciple for wisdom. The other is Punna, son of Mantani, praised to the Buddha by the monks of his home country.

Sariputta wants to meet him. So he follows Punna into a grove called the Blind Men's Wood, sits down under a tree a little way off, and when the afternoon is ending, walks over and starts asking questions.
Punna has no idea who he's talking to.

teach.h: WHY DO YOU LIVE THE HOLY LIFE?
teach.b: In the twenty-fourth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, Sariputta asks: why do you live the holy life? For pure virtue? No.
For a pure mind? No. For pure view?
No. Down a list of seven purities, Punna says no to every one. Then what for?
For final release without clinging, Punna says. Then is final release the same as pure virtue? No.

teach.h: SEVEN CHARIOTS FROM SAVATTHI TO SAKETA
teach.b: Is it something apart from all seven? Also no. So Punna gives a picture.
King Pasenadi lives in Savatthi and has urgent business in Saketa, a long way off. He sets out seven chariots in relay along the road.
He rides the first to the second, climbs down, rides the second to the third, and so on, until the seventh brings him to the palace gate in Saketa.
If someone at the gate asks, did you come here from Savatthi in this chariot, and the king says yes, that's not quite true. The honest answer names the whole relay.

teach.h: EACH ONE ONLY REACHES THE NEXT
teach.b: Each chariot only had to reach the next one. That's how the seven purities work, Punna says. Pure virtue is for the sake of a pure mind.
A pure mind is for the sake of pure view. And so on down the road, until the last purity carries you to release.

teach.h: NONE IS THE GOAL; EACH SERVES THE NEXT
teach.b: None of them is the goal.
Each is there for the sake of the next. Then the two men learn each other's names, and each praises the other.

how: In Theravada teaching, the seven purifications from this discourse later shaped Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga, where a practitioner's progress is described stage by stage, each purity resting on the one before.

o: a royal escort guarding a king's travels
seven stages, each one carrying you to the next
a well-known race run at the king's festival

games.q: who's who on the road — tap the pairs.
p: asks the questions under the tree
for the sake of a pure mind

s: Punna says the goal of the holy life is pure virtue
he says no to all seven purities: the goal is final release without clinging.
the king could honestly say one chariot brought him
the honest answer names the whole relay: each chariot only reached the next.
in Punna's answer, each purity is for the sake of the next
pure virtue for a pure mind, and so on, all the way to release.

games.q: you're King Pasenadi, arriving at the palace gate in Saketa. someone asks: did this chariot bring you all the way from Savatthi? what's the honest answer?
o: no: seven chariots, each to the next.
no chariot brought me; I walked.
games.why: Punna's point: the last chariot only covered the last stretch. the whole relay brought the king, the way seven purities carry someone to release.

practice: Think of something long you're in the middle of, a recovery, a degree, a hard year, a habit you're rebuilding, and picture only the next chariot: the one small stretch actually in front of you this week.
Then sit with the breath, one breath as one stage, and when the mind runs ahead to the palace gate, bring it back to this chariot.

wordCard.voice: Relay chariots. Seven purities, each one there to carry you to the next, until the last brings you to release.

orig.note: Pali ratha: chariot. the discourse is called the Rathavinita Sutta, the relay of chariots.

carryVoice: Your line: one stage at a time. The road is long; the next chariot is close. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 24, Rathavinita Sutta (the relay chariots)
